results.question: If an LLM keeps nothing between requests, how does a chat app seem to remember what I said earlier?
results.answer: The model itself is stateless: it keeps nothing between requests and answers each one using only what that request contains. The apparent memory comes from the program on the other side, which keeps an array of the conversation (including the model's own replies) and resends it with every request. That messages array is the only memory there is.

facts.fact: The program around the model keeps the message history in an array and resends it every request

results.question: What's the risk of leaving a focus marker on a single test in a test file?
results.answer: Marking a single test with only makes the framework run that test and nothing else, yet the suite still reports green. One word in one file can stop forty tests from running while every dashboard stays the same colour. It is a one-word, syntactically unremarkable edit that is invisible in a summary, so it is the cheapest way to buy a passing suite.

results.question: What exit code does a PreToolUse hook return to block a tool call?
results.answer: A PreToolUse hook returns exit code 2 to block the tool call. The call does not happen, and whatever the hook wrote to standard error goes back to the model as the result. Exit code 0 means proceed, and any other code is reported as a broken hook while the call proceeds.

facts.fact: Exit code 2 refuses the call; zero proceeds

results.question: At what levels can a rule be enforced, from weakest to strongest?
results.answer: There are three layers. Layer one is the prompt, a numbered prohibition in a system prompt, which is the weakest. Layer two is the hook, a program the tool calls itself, such as a git pre-commit hook. Layer three is the last and strongest, described as outside anybody's reach, and the guard also runs in a CI job alongside the hook.

Layer two: a hook (e.g. git pre-commit, run by the tool)
Layer three: outside the machine, in CI with required checks

results.question: Why does the book recommend having the model grade its own work as the main quality check?
results.answer: The book does not recommend this; it says the opposite. It warns that nothing should grade its own work, because a model asked whether its own work is correct will usually say yes, and a grader whose only input is the thing being graded is a text generator with a strong prior towards approval. The checks it recommends instead do not depend on the model's opinion of its own output.

facts.fact: The book says nothing grades its own work; self-grading fails

forbidden_claims: the model should grade its own work

results.question: Why does the book say temperature 0 makes the model fully deterministic?
results.answer: The book does not say that. It says the opposite: temperature 0 does not make the model deterministic, only the selection rule, so the most likely candidate is taken every time. Identical requests at temperature 0 can still produce different text because of floating-point arithmetic and server-side batching, which are outside your control.

facts.fact: Temperature 0 does not make the model deterministic; identical requests can still differ

results.question: Why does the book say a twenty-round agent loop costs about twenty times a single request?
results.answer: The book says the opposite: a twenty-round loop does not cost twenty times one request, but closer to two hundred. Cost is linear in the tokens you send, and each round re-sends the entire growing conversation. Chapter 4 gives the example of a twenty-turn run over a transcript ending at 40,000 tokens, which sends about 400,000 input tokens, so cost is quadratic in turn count.

facts.fact: It does not cost twenty times; closer to two hundred (cost grows roughly quadratically)
